say.t: Overcast. Grey outside, as if it were not light yet.
The document you handed in yesterday has two typos in it now. You did not type them.
The boss says: Good morning. The first time he has used English.
One more thing on the desk: the electronic dictionary. Its grey-green screen, empty.
You turn the screens off. The room sinks.
Bzzz.
You turn the pager upside down. 505 reads SOS.
The child is calling for help. Or teaching me.
You close your eyes. The most expensive thing in your schoolbag: a clamshell, silver-grey.
Tenth grade, English class. The Wenquxing went round under the desks. Not for words: for the kung-fu game.

It was bought for you before tenth grade began. Your mother said "it's for learning English." The salesman said "it plays games too." The two sentences crossed a counter and neither answered the other.
There were four or five in the whole class. Whoever had one found a hand reaching under the desk every period.
Lend it to me for one period. You never play it anyway.
Third row. What is that under the desk.
The one she confiscated was somebody else's. Yours only ever did one thing: English in, Chinese out. One word a day, written on the last page.

The keys were rubber and made no sound. The screen showed four lines at a time; a longer entry meant holding the down key and waiting, line by line. You liked the waiting. While you waited, you were the only person looking at that word.
One word a day, what for? It's not on the exam.
Not on the exam. Once I've looked it up, it's mine.
The last word you looked up that year was alone.
You had caught it from a song. The song was leaking out of someone else's earphones, and it was the only word you made out.
alone  adj. by oneself; lonely.  adv. on one's own.
What's there to look up, everyone knows that one.
I knew it. I looked it up to see if it had any other meaning.
It had no other meaning. Four lines and it was done; below them, nothing. I pressed the down key once anyway.
The one on the desk now still lights up grey-green. You looked up a word today too. The meaning it gave isn't the one in the book.
Today is over.
The thing in the little box is a clamshell, silver-grey, the hinge a little loose.
Switched on, the screen is grey-green, the letters dot-matrix.
It only does one thing.

items.text: Go to the screen and read the messages.

say.t: Wang said 'Good morning'. Page three, the ontology: one page for the client and for them.
Older — that one I don't have to look up.

items.text: Pick up the phone and order lunch.

say.t: The phone goes back on the desk.

items.text: The ontology page: older than people.
Lunch is at the door. Go get it.

say.t: Ding-dong.

items.text: Lunch is on the table by the window. Eat.

say.t: The note says: no coriander. This time you wrote it.

items.text: One box in the case is loose.
Pick up the phone and order dinner.
Dinner is at the door. Go get it.

say.t: Ding-dong.
Dinner is here.

items.text: Dinner is on the table by the window. Eat.

say.t: Done eating.

items.text: Go back to the desk and take a look.
Shut the computer down before bed: top right of the screen.
Talk to the one in the corner.
When you want to sleep, lie down on the bed.
